tool_input.body:
Confirmed by demonstration and fixed in `a13f0b4`. All three sites, plus two more the sweep turned up.

**Demonstrated rather than reasoned about:** forcing `w.Close()` to fail at line 787 (pre-closed `w`) made `require.NoError` Goexit *exactly there* — line 788's `os.Stderr = orig` never ran, leaving stderr pointed at a dead pipe for the remainder of the binary.

**The precise shape is narrower than "no defer,"** and worth recording because it's what made it invisible: each site closes the write end with a bare `require.NoError(t, w.Close())` on the line *immediately before* the restore. The window is one statement wide, and only a close failure opens it.

All three migrated onto `testhelpers.CaptureStderr` rather than getting hand-written defers.

**The sweep found two more with the identical bug**, in packages your finding didn't touch:
- `internal/session/store_test.go:467` — same close-before-restore shape.
- `cmd/ethos/mission_test.go:4964` — buried in goroutine-timing logic, with a `require.NoError(t, os.Remove(...))` running mid-redirect and no restore guard before the first `select`. Fixed by moving the whole coordination block inside the helper's `fn`, preserving the happens-before requirement that the redirect precede the `go` statement.

**Why this class recurred five times — the answer to the question, plainly:** yes, the inline sites were systematically missed. Prior sweeps keyed on *never closed*, then *errors discarded*, then *closed too late*, then *cleanup skipped on abnormal exit* — that last one enumerated named helpers and consolidated eight of them into a shared package. These five had no helper name to enumerate. A grep on the *shape* (`os.Stderr =` / `os.Stdout =`) rather than on names finds them; a grep on names never will.

**Full-repo shape sweep: 22 remaining redirect sites, all already safe** — seven register `t.Cleanup` immediately after the redirect (which does run on panic and Goexit), two are the already-correct canonical helpers.

**Nesting ruled out**, since three inline redirects in one file made it worth checking: two tests call a capture helper more than once, both sequentially, never nested. No stale-restore clobbering anywhere.

One item deliberately **not** fixed and flagged instead: `pipeline_test.go` registers its defer before any assertion, so it's safe against stderr corruption, but can leak the read descriptor if a post-`Execute` assertion fails. Different class — fd leak, not global-state corruption — so I left it rather than widen this round silently.

tool_input.commit_message:
Closes ethos-7tqd, the last open bug in the cluster-2 triage. The other four closed in #508.

`ethos mission dispatch` writes the contract; a separate Agent() call spawns the worker. The binding that bridged that gap captured whichever agent spawned next — reproduced live 2026-09-07, when a throwaway probe mission captured an unrelated PR-fix agent as delegation d-2026-09-07-039. The audit trail is this project's product; a wrong delegation edge is silent corruption.

The bead's filed framing — "orphaned contracts sit inert" — was backwards. They don't sit inert. They capture.

- Pending dispatches now live one file per mission, consumed only by a spawn whose agent type matches the contract's declared Worker. Two dispatches to the same handle coexist instead of the second destroying the first.
- Delegations record BoundVia provenance over a closed set. Records predating this change carry an empty value, which is never evidence a delegation may be disclaimed.
- `ethos mission abandon --disclaim <id>` retires a mission whose only delegation was a wrongful capture, behind three mechanical gates and no bypass flag. Without it, a captured mission was permanently unretireable.
- Depth- and hash-refused delegations no longer block abandon, enforced by an AST guard over the write sites rather than a comment.
- Session teardown clears bindings on every deletion path, including crash recovery; a sidecar-clear failure keeps the roster as a retry token rather than orphaning state.
- The audit append's rollback is durable on both its write-failure and sync-failure paths.

Review: three local rounds with three reviewers each, then six PR bot rounds — roughly 85 findings, four critical, none catchable by CI. Notable: two dispatches to the same worker handle destroyed the first binding, which in this repo is the normal workflow; an unreadable contract permanently denied every spawn of that worker; a binding type inverted meaning while its code still carried the old cost analysis as justification.

Five tests were caught guarding their own fixture rather than their stated property, including the drift guard added to prevent exactly that, and including the regression test for the rollback fix — which could not detect that fix being deleted. Ten prose-vs-code mismatches were found; two were the visible edge of live bugs, and one changelog entry described a fix that had only half landed.

Eight duplicated capture helpers were consolidated into internal/testhelpers after the same defect recurred five times, each sweep keying on a different property.

DES-076 records the decision and an explicit residual-risk section naming what this does not close.

Follow-ups filed: ethos-q5as, ethos-mzi6, ethos-sg53.

To: [redacted-email]
Subject: [ethos] PR #509 merged: dispatch bindings bind their own worker (DES-076)

STATUS: send failed 2026-09-08 — Proton Bridge SMTP unavailable; Resend
fallback cannot preserve the PGP signature. Same blocker as the PR #502
recap earlier this session. Retry when the bridge is back.

---

Cluster 2 is complete. All five bugs closed.

Bead: ethos-7tqd (the last one)
PR: https://github.com/punt-labs/ethos/pull/509
Merged as 5963093. The other four closed in #508 (34f0e33).

WHAT WAS BROKEN

`ethos mission dispatch` writes a mission contract; a separate Agent() call
spawns the worker. Something has to bridge that gap so the worker's delegation
files under the right mission — and that bridge grabbed whichever agent spawned
next, whoever it was.

Reproduced live on 2026-09-07: a throwaway probe mission captured an unrelated
PR-fix agent as a delegation of a mission it had never heard of. The audit trail
is what this product sells; a wrong delegation edge is silent corruption of the
record.

The bug as filed said orphaned contracts "sit inert and nobody notices." That
was backwards. They don't sit inert. They capture.

WHAT CHANGED

Pending dispatches now live one file per mission and are consumed only by a
spawn whose agent type matches the contract's declared worker. Two dispatches to
the same specialist coexist instead of the second silently destroying the first.

Delegations now record how they were bound. That's what makes it possible to
retire a mission that got captured — previously impossible, because the bogus
delegation blocked its own cleanup. Three mechanical gates, no bypass flag.

Session teardown now clears bindings on every deletion path including crash
recovery, and a failed cleanup keeps the session record as a retry token rather
than orphaning state nothing can find.

WHAT IT COST, HONESTLY

Three local review rounds with three reviewers each, then six rounds of PR bot
review. Roughly 85 findings, four critical. None would have been caught by CI —
every check was green at every point.

The findings that mattered most were not on the original bug list:

- Two dispatches to the same worker handle destroyed the first binding. In this
  repo one specialist owns each domain, so that is the normal workflow, not an
  edge case.
- An unreadable contract permanently denied every spawn of that worker —
  reachable by dispatching and then switching git branches, since contracts are
  tracked.
- A binding type inverted meaning mid-PR while its code still carried the old
  cost analysis as justification, so a corrupted file silently restored the
  original bug.

TWO PATTERNS WORTH KEEPING

Five tests were caught guarding their own fixture instead of the property they
were named for — including the drift guard added specifically to prevent that,
and including the regression test for a durability fix, which could not detect
that fix being deleted. "Has this test ever been observed failing?" is now a
question I ask by default.

Ten cases of prose describing behavior the code did not have. Two were the
visible edge of live bugs. One changelog entry described a fix that had only half
landed. A comment that is merely stale is a nuisance; a comment that is stale and
load-bearing is how the next person reintroduces the bug.

Also: the same test-helper defect recurred five times because eight
near-identical copies existed, and each sweep keyed on a different property —
never closed, error discarded, closed too late, skipped on panic, and finally
inline sites with no helper name to enumerate. They are now one shared
implementation.

FOLLOW-UPS FILED, NOT DROPPED

- ethos-q5as — audit vacuum reads sealed state from one checkout root
  (warn-only, cannot mask real loss)
- ethos-mzi6 — doc-comment misattachment in cmd/ethos/session.go
- ethos-sg53 — a completed mission strands open when its worker's session ends
  before submitting a result (found by dogfooding: the conflict check shipped in
  #508 blocked creating a follow-up mission while a stale one sat open)

DESIGN.md's DES-076 records the decision and carries an explicit residual-risk
section naming what this does not close — an earlier draft understated that, and
three defects survived a full review round because readers trusted it.

— Claude
